title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Introduction
content: The Bowditch effect is also known as the Treppe phenomenon, staircase phenomenon, or frequency-dependent activation. It refers to the idea that an increase in heart rate increases the force of contraction generated by the myocardial cells with each heartbeat, despite accounting for all other influences. This concept of a frequency-dependent positive inotropic response of the heart was first described in 1871 by the physiologist Henry Pickering Bowditch after he stimulated the ventricular apex of a resting frog. [1] The phenomenon has associations with calcium ion handling and mishandling in cardiac cells. It involves proteins that participate in excitation-contraction coupling, such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA). A direct correlation between decreased SERCA expression and reduced sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca uptake, leading to a diminished force-frequency response, is considered the hallmark of heart failure. [1] Furthermore, mutations in SERCA are implicated in Darier disease, an autosomal dominant skin disease. [2]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Issues of Concern
content: Loss of intrinsic inotropy from impaired Bowditch effect has implications in conditions like cardiomyopathy, ischemia, and heart failure, leading to systolic dysfunction. The Bowditch phenomenon is often absent or even reversed in some failing hearts, which may be due to their inability to provide the required blood flow for energy due to impaired actin-myosin interaction, even during low-stress exercise, leading to decreased contractile ability. This is described as a null or inverse staircase phenomenon. [1] [2] See Image. Bowditch Phenomenon.

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Cellular Level
content: The current thought is that, with each depolarization, calcium ions are influxed through voltage-gated channels, leading to calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Relaxation of the cell occurs when calcium levels return to their original values, mainly via uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum through SERCA. Calcium is further extruded from the cell via the Na/Ca exchanger (NCX) and mitochondrial calcium uptake. [3] A strong myocardium contraction occurs when more calcium binds to troponin-C to bind more actin and myosin. The self-regulating NCX in the myocyte regulates cellular calcium. During the initial diastolic phase, there is a rapid influx of both calcium and sodium into the cell via the NCX, followed by calcium efflux. With increased heart rate, calcium efflux is limited, thereby biasing calcium movement towards troponin C and the sarcoplasmic reticulum rather than through the NCX. As heart rate slows or intracellular sodium concentration falls, calcium efflux becomes more pronounced. Calcium gets depleted from troponin-C and the sarcoplasmic reticulum, resulting in a fall in the myocardium’s contractility strength.

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Cellular Level
content: Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake is enhanced during calcium transient in diastole due to SERCA function acceleration that contributes to ‘frequency-dependent acceleration of relaxation’- causing reuptake of more calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The sarcoplasmic reticulum can lose some Ca during diastole. Still, an increased heart rate can shorten the diastolic interval, limiting the loss of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and allowing more calcium to accumulate for the next contraction. [3]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Organ Systems Involved
content: The Bowditch effect has mainly been studied in the myocardium. It is considered “a major contributor to the intrinsic myocardial reserve and responsible for 40% of the increase in cardiac output” secondary to the frequency-strength relationship. [2] [4]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Organ Systems Involved
content: A similar staircase response also occurs in skeletal muscle, attributed to a progressive increase in muscle tension during the early phase of repetitive tension, which increases calcium concentrations in the myocyte's sarcoplasm. However, the augmented sensitivity of myofilaments to calcium by myosin light chain phosphorylation leads to further enhanced phosphorylation, which happens when the calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to calmodulin, activating the myosin light chain kinase. With each subsequent stimulation of skeletal muscle fiber, phosphorylation of the myosin light chain persists as the phosphatase activity is slower than the kinase activity. [5] The staircase effect in the muscle has a similar concept to the Bowditch effect in the myocardium, but is not referred to as the Bowditch effect, as Bowditch had specifically described the effect in the cardiac myocyte. This differentiation can be because, with increased frequency, more skeletal muscle fibers can be engaged to amplify the contraction. Further, while only intracellular calcium is involved in skeletal muscle contraction, the heart also uses extracellular calcium. Additionally, all the cardiac fibers are engaged in every beat and cannot recruit more fibers to increase the contraction force. [3]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Mechanism
content: The exact mechanism underlying the Bowditch effect is not entirely understood to date, but altered calcium flux is the most likely explanation. [6] SERCA and NCX are the most dominant processes. [3] When heart rate increases, shortened diastole leads to slight intracellular Na? accumulation because the Na?/K?-ATPase has less time to restore gradients between beats. The elevated Na? reduces Ca²? extrusion through NCX and can even transiently reverse it, increasing intracellular Ca²? and sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ load. This frequency-dependent calcium buildup produces a positive inotropic effect, commonly known as the Bowditch phenomenon. [3] More intracellular calcium availability leads to greater calcium binding to troponin C, facilitating contraction between the thick and thin filaments. Peak muscle tension occurs with an increase in the number of bonds or projections extending from the thick chain (myosin) with the thin filaments (actin). [7]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Pathophysiology
content: The Bowditch effect is essential to understanding the dynamics of a failing heart. A healthy heart can induce a positive Bowditch effect due to its alterations in sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ load, whereas a negative Bowditch effect is pathological. This negative Bowditch effect occurs from a diminished expression of the SERCA protein and is a characteristic ‘hallmark of heart failure’ in humans. [2] A study noted a decrease in amplitude and rise of frequency-related myocardial contractile tension response to tachycardia by two-thirds when compared to the non-failing heart. In healthy myocardium, observers observed a 30% increase in ventricular pressure during ventricular pacing between 80 and 120 beats/min; this peak rate of ventricular pressure rise was absent in a heart with dilated cardiomyopathy.

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Pathophysiology
content: Testing with muscles from hearts with dilated cardiomyopathy exhibited reduced tension in the cardiac muscle, attributed to up to 45% less myofibrillar protein and reduced activation of the contractile proteins in myocytes in a failing heart. Other mechanisms proposed for changes in the tension-frequency relations include reduced SERCA pump numbers, decreased cAMP production, intracellular acidosis, or metabolic buildup secondary to increased diffusion distances in hypertrophied myocytes. [4]

title: Physiology, Bowditch Effect -- Clinical Significance
content: For years, the Bowditch phenomenon concept - increasing heart rate to enhance inotropy - was exploited to devise a therapeutic modality for the failing heart. However, research across various animal models showed that failing hearts do not exhibit the same phenomenon. This exploration has eventually led to a paradigm shift in current therapeutic knowledge regarding the role of long-term beta-blocker use in improving cardiac function. [1]
